title: WHY DID GOD USE SHOCKING SEXUAL LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE ISRAEL’S IDOLATRY?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD USE SHOCKING SEXUAL LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE ISRAEL’S IDOLATRY?

The disturbing words of Ezekiel weren’t written to entertain dirty minds. They were meant to expose wandering hearts—and once you understand what God was saying, you may never look at idolatry the same way again.
There are passages in the Bible that comfort you.
There are passages that strengthen you.
And then there are passages that make you stop reading and stare at the page.
Ezekiel 16 and Ezekiel 23 are among them.
The language becomes so sexually graphic, so emotionally violent, so uncomfortable that a modern reader may instinctively wonder:
Why is this even in the Bible?
Why would the holy God speak about His covenant people using imagery of prostitution, adultery, nakedness, lust, lovers, breasts, sexual desire, and marital betrayal?
And Ezekiel 23 goes further still.
Far further.
The Hebrew becomes deliberately disturbing.
There is a line many churches would probably never read aloud on Sunday morning.
Yet God permitted it to remain in Scripture.
Why?
Because sometimes we sanitize the very sins that are destroying us.
We call idolatry a “distraction.”
God called it betrayal.
We call compromise a “season.”
God showed Israel an unfaithful marriage.
We say, “I’ve just been distant from God lately.”
Scripture sometimes describes that distance with the vocabulary of adultery.
That difference should make us uncomfortable.
Because perhaps one reason Ezekiel shocks us is that God takes spiritual unfaithfulness more seriously than we do.
And before going any further, something must be made absolutely clear.

These chapters should never become an excuse for vulgar preaching, sexual humiliation, hatred toward women, or treating victims of sexual violence as morally responsible for what was done to them. Modern scholars have rightly pointed out how troubling the gendered violence and sexual rhetoric of Ezekiel 16 and 23 can be, and interpreters have disagreed over how some elements of these metaphors should be understood. The sexual imagery must therefore be handled carefully rather than sensationalized.
The woman in Ezekiel's metaphor is not “women” as a class.
The prophetic target is covenant-breaking Israel and Judah.
Ezekiel himself tells us who the characters represent.
In Ezekiel 23, two sisters appear: Oholah and Oholibah.
The Hebrew names are אָהֳלָה (Oholah) and אָהֳלִיבָה (Oholibah).
Then Scripture removes the mystery:
“Samaria is Oholah and Jerusalem Oholibah.”
These are personified cities and kingdoms.
This is prophetic metaphor.
And once that is understood, the disturbing language begins revealing something terrifyingly beautiful about the heart of God.
Because adultery hurts only where covenant exists.
Betrayal hurts only where love existed first.
You cannot betray someone who never loved you.
And that is where Ezekiel 16 begins.
Not with prostitution.
Not with judgment.
Not with sexual scandal.
With grace.
Jerusalem is pictured as an abandoned infant.
Unwanted.
Unwashed.
Unprotected.
Lying helplessly in blood.
Nobody has compassion.
Nobody rescues her.
Then God comes.
He gives life.
He cleanses her.
He clothes her.
He adorns her.
He provides for her.
And eventually the imagery becomes covenantal and marital.
God says that He entered into covenant with her and she became His.
The Hebrew word underneath this covenant idea is בְּרִית — berit.
Covenant.
That matters enormously.
Israel did not rescue herself and then impress God enough to become His people.
God found her.
God chose her.
God covered her.
God provided for her.
God beautified her.
Grace came first.
And then comes one of the most devastating turns in prophetic literature:
“But you trusted in your beauty…”
There it is.
The tragedy of the human heart in a sentence.
She began admiring the gifts until she forgot the Giver.
The beauty God gave became the beauty she trusted.
The resources God supplied became resources she used against Him.
The blessings that should have produced worship became instruments of rebellion.
Then Ezekiel uses the Hebrew vocabulary of prostitution.
The important root is זנה — zanah.
Depending on grammatical form and context, it carries the idea of engaging in prostitution or acting promiscuously.
But in Ezekiel's prophetic metaphor, we cannot simply flatten that word into literal sexual behavior.
Ezekiel explicitly connects this “prostitution” with idols, pagan worship, and relationships with foreign powers.
That is why the language is so fierce.
Israel wasn't merely violating regulations.
She was violating relationship.
Imagine a husband giving his wife a beautiful necklace because he loves her.
Then imagine her wearing that necklace while pursuing another lover.
The problem isn't the necklace.
The horror is that a gift of love has become an accessory to betrayal.
That is essentially the accusation of Ezekiel 16.
God had given Israel gold, silver, clothing, food, beauty, security and covenant privilege.
Then Israel took what God had provided and devoted it to idols.
And suddenly the ancient prophecy becomes frighteningly modern.
Because we can do exactly the same thing.
God gives someone intelligence.
They build a life in which they no longer need Him.
God gives someone influence.
They become addicted to applause.
God gives someone money.
Money becomes their security.
God gives someone beauty.
Beauty becomes their identity.
God gives someone a relationship.
The relationship becomes more important than obedience.
God gives someone ministry.
And eventually the ministry becomes more important than God.
God gives someone a platform supposedly built for Jesus.
Then slowly...
quietly...
almost invisibly...
Jesus becomes a tool for building the platform.
That is idolatry wearing church clothes.
And this is why Ezekiel's language cannot safely remain locked in ancient Jerusalem.
The idols change.
The human heart doesn't.
We may never bow before Baal.
We can still bow before approval.
We may never burn incense to Asherah.
We can still sacrifice our integrity for success.
We may never construct a pagan shrine.

We can still build an altar inside ourselves where money, sex, romance, politics, reputation, career, comfort, entertainment, influence, family—or even ministry—receives the trust that belongs to God.
An idol is not merely a statue.
It is something created that begins receiving what belongs ultimately to the Creator.
Your deepest trust.
Your obedience.
Your identity.
Your hope.
Your fear.
Your devotion.
Your functional worship.
And sometimes you don't discover your idol by asking what you love.
You discover it by asking what you cannot imagine losing.
That question may hurt.
Let it.
Ezekiel was supposed to hurt.
But now we arrive at the passage that has made generations of readers recoil.
Ezekiel 23 intensifies the imagery dramatically.

The prophet describes Israel's attraction toward foreign powers through explicitly sexual imagery. In verse 20, the Hebrew text uses startling bodily language, including בְּשַׂר — basar, literally “flesh,” which in context functions as a sexual reference.
The comparison that follows is intentionally crude.
Modern translations differ in how explicitly they render it.
But the shock is there in Hebrew.
We should neither pretend otherwise nor linger over it voyeuristically.
The question is not:
“How graphic can we make this?”
The better question is:
“Why would prophetic Scripture speak this way?”
Because Israel had made rebellion attractive.
God's rhetoric tears the perfume off the idol.
Israel looked toward powerful nations and saw strength, security and desirability.
God exposes the lust underneath that political and spiritual dependence.
What Israel romanticized, Ezekiel makes grotesque.
That is one of idolatry's greatest tricks.
It makes slavery look beautiful before the chains close.
Pornography promises intimacy and produces isolation.
Greed promises security and produces endless hunger.
Human approval promises belonging and produces anxiety.
Pride promises greatness and makes repentance unbearable.
Bitterness promises justice while quietly chaining you to the person who wounded you.
Secret sin promises relief.
Then demands secrecy.
Then demands repetition.
Then demands more.
And eventually the thing you thought you controlled begins controlling you.
This is why biblical idolatry is not merely about statues.
It is about misplaced desire.
Misplaced trust.
Misplaced dependence.
Misplaced worship.
Israel sought from other gods and nations what she was supposed to receive ultimately from Yahweh.
And here is the part that should break something open inside us:
God's jealousy in covenant Scripture is not the insecurity of a needy deity desperate for attention.
God does not need us to complete Him.
Rather, covenant jealousy reflects the exclusive relationship to which His people belong.
The tragedy of idolatry is therefore not simply that God is denied something.
The worshiper is giving himself to something that cannot save him.
That is why idols are cruel masters.
They take sacrifices.
But they cannot resurrect anyone.
They demand devotion.
But they cannot forgive sin.
They promise identity.
But they cannot tell you who you were created to be.
They can consume your life.
They cannot give you eternal life.
And maybe your idol isn't something obviously wicked.
Maybe it is the person whose approval determines whether you feel valuable.
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ but you're terrified to surrender.
Maybe it is the secret browser history nobody knows about.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe attention.
Maybe your image.
Maybe achievement.
Maybe your children.
Maybe your ministry.
Maybe being right.
Maybe being wanted.
Maybe being noticed.
Maybe being admired.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something you have repeatedly promised God you would surrender.
Then you went back.
Again.
And again.
And again.
You deleted it.
Reinstalled it.
Confessed it.
Returned to it.
Cried about it.
Hid it.
Promised God.
Broke the promise.
And now shame whispers:
After everything you've done, why would God still want you?
This is where the Gospel enters the scandal.
Because Ezekiel 16 does not end where many people assume it should.
Judgment is real.
Sin is not minimized.
Covenant betrayal has consequences.
Yet near the end, God speaks again about covenant.
He declares that He will remember His covenant.
That does not make the rebellion insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
The Bible's answer to human unfaithfulness is not that human beings eventually become good enough to deserve another chance.
The story moves toward something infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ.
The One who does not merely expose adulterous hearts.
He comes to redeem sinners.
At the cross, God does not pretend our spiritual betrayal never happened.
Sin is dealt with.
Judgment is not waved away as though holiness doesn't matter.
Christ bears sin.
And resurrection announces that sin, death, guilt and condemnation do not get the final word over everyone who belongs to Him.
This is why the Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up and maybe God will take you back.”
The Gospel announces what God has done in Christ and calls sinners to repent and believe.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance.
It is not cosmetic Christianity.
Not religious damage control.
Not learning how to hide your idols better.
Repentance is a turning.
A changed mind that results in changed direction.
You stop defending the thing separating you from God.
You bring it into the light.
You call it what God calls it.
You turn toward Christ.
And here is where scandal becomes grace.
Jesus does not merely rewrite reputations.
He transforms people.
The sexually broken can be redeemed.
The proud can be humbled.
The addicted can begin walking in freedom.
The hypocrite can confess.
The bitter can forgive.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The wanderer can return.
The sinner can be washed.
Not because sin wasn't serious.
Because the blood of Christ is sufficient.
There is another Greek word worth remembering:
χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Not divine permission to continue worshiping idols.
Grace rescues us from them.
Grace does not say, “Your betrayal doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Christ paid what you could never pay, so stop running from the One who came to save you.”
Maybe that is why you needed to encounter Ezekiel's uncomfortable language today.
Not because God wanted to disgust you.
Because He wanted to wake you.
Some sins survive because we keep giving them polite names.
We call greed ambition.
Lust loneliness.
Pride confidence.
Cowardice wisdom.
Bitterness discernment.
Compromise complexity.
Idolatry priorities.
And spiritual coldness “being busy.”
But there comes a moment when grace loves you enough to stop flattering you.
So be honest before God.
What has your heart?
Not your Sunday vocabulary.
Your heart.
What do you run toward when you hurt?
What do you fear losing most?
Whose approval controls you?
What determines whether you feel valuable?
What do you repeatedly choose even when obedience to Jesus requires surrendering it?
What occupies your imagination when everything becomes quiet?
What has become so important that you would rather compromise with God than lose it?
Don't answer publicly unless you should.
But answer God.
And if this article exposed something hidden, you don't need to tell strangers every detail.
Your comment might become the sentence another struggling believer sees at midnight and realizes:
I'm not the only one fighting.
That matters.
So does sharing this.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly losing a war nobody knows they're fighting.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.
It doesn't.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be bought.
Your support helps us keep creating and sharing Scripture-centered resources designed to point people toward Jesus, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation.
If these words convicted you, don't merely admire the conviction.
Respond to it.
But above everything else—
come back to Jesus.
Because the deepest message of Ezekiel's shocking imagery is not that sinners are too filthy to return.
It is that sin is far uglier than we imagined...
and covenant grace is far more astonishing than we deserved.
The idol you keep running toward will eventually ask you to sacrifice something it can never give back.
Jesus gave Himself to rescue people who had nothing worthy to offer Him.
So when your scandal tells you the story is finished, remember the empty tomb.
Grace still knows how to write on pages shame thought were already ruined.
